body:
## feat(booking): integrate owner availability

### Contexto

O availability engine já está consolidado no backend pelas migrations 026–028:

- **026** — geração autoritativa de disponibilidade;
- **027** — enforcement transacional e proteção contra concorrência;
- **028** — reader autenticado `get_owner_availability` para criação e reagendamento do owner.

Até esta etapa, o fluxo remoto do owner ainda mantinha parte da decisão temporal no frontend, incluindo seleção livre de data/hora/duração e reconstrução de timestamps no browser.

Esta PR integra a Agenda do owner ao availability engine já publicado, fazendo o frontend consumir os slots finais fornecidos pelo backend sem alterar a arquitetura de escrita existente.

---

### Implementação

O fluxo remoto do owner agora consulta:

`public.get_owner_availability(...)`

utilizando:

- `service_id`;
- `barber_id`;
- data local operacional;
- `appointment_id = NULL` para criação;
- `appointment_id` real para reagendamento.

O frontend não envia `barbershop_id` e não deriva tenant.

O tenant continua sendo determinado exclusivamente pelo backend a partir da identidade autenticada.

Nenhuma migration ou RPC foi criada ou modificada nesta PR.

---

### Criação de agendamento

No fluxo remoto:

`serviço → barbeiro → data → availability → slot → writer`

A UI agora:

- consulta os slots finais da 028;
- distingue loading, empty e error;
- invalida a seleção ao alterar serviço, barbeiro ou data;
- protege contra respostas assíncronas obsoletas;
- utiliza exatamente `start_at/end_at` retornados pelo backend;
- não recalcula `end_at` pela duração;
- não reconstrói o instante a partir de data/hora exibidas;
- não faz fallback remoto para disponibilidade local em caso de erro.

Após criação bem-sucedida, a agenda autenticada é relida para receber os UUIDs persistidos pelo banco.

O INSERT existente do owner foi intencionalmente preservado nesta PR.

---

### Reagendamento

Para appointment existente, a consulta utiliza:

`p_appointment_id = appointment.id`

A autoexclusão do próprio appointment continua sendo responsabilidade da migration 028.

O frontend não replica regras de conflito nem tenta remover manualmente o appointment atual da ocupação.

Mudanças de:

- serviço;
- barbeiro;
- data;

invalidam o slot anterior e provocam nova consulta de disponibilidade.

Outros appointments continuam sendo considerados pelo backend normalmente.

---

### Identidade por ID

O fluxo remoto deixa de depender de nomes para determinar a identidade de serviço e barbeiro.

A seleção utiliza:

- `service_id`;
- `barber_id`;
- `appointment.id`.

Nomes permanecem apenas como labels de apresentação.

Isso também evita associação incorreta quando existem profissionais homônimos.

Ao abrir uma criação a partir de um barbeiro selecionado na Agenda, o respectivo `barber_id` é propagado até:

`Agenda → modal → availability → submit`

sem substituição pelo primeiro barbeiro do catálogo.

---

### Duração autoritativa

Para appointments remotos vinculados a serviço, o frontend não utiliza duração editável como autoridade temporal.

O intervalo selecionado é exatamente:

`start_at → end_at`

retornado pelo availability engine.

A duração autoritativa continua derivada do catálogo de serviços no backend.

A migration 027 permanece responsável por rejeitar qualquer escrita incompatível com o contrato.

---

### Edição não temporal

Alterações que não representam reagendamento não reconstruem o intervalo do appointment.

Exemplos:

- nome do cliente;
- telefone;
- observação.

Nesses casos:

- `start_at` original é preservado;
- `end_at` original é preservado;
- não é realizada consulta desnecessária de disponibilidade;
- timestamps não passam por nova conversão de timezone;
- precisão existente é mantida.

Uma edição textual não é transformada implicitamente em reagendamento.

---

### Timezone operacional

A Agenda remota passa a utilizar `operational_timezone` como referência de calendário e apresentação.

O frontend:

- não utiliza `financial_timezone` como fallback;
- não utiliza timezone do navegador como autoridade da agenda remota;
- não reconstrói timestamps a partir do horário formatado;
- preserva os `timestamptz` absolutos recebidos.

A data inicial automática também considera o timezone operacional.

Exemplo coberto:

`2030-10-01T01:00:00Z`

em:

`America/Recife`

corresponde ao dia operacional:

`2030-09-30`

Uma data escolhida manualmente pelo owner não é sobrescrita posteriormente pelo carregamento do timezone.

Quando o timezone operacional não está configurado, o fluxo remoto não inventa um timezone padrão nem converte silenciosamente para disponibilidade local.

---

### Proteção contra stale requests

Consultas de disponibilidade são protegidas contra respostas fora de ordem.

Exemplo:

`request A → troca de serviço → request B → B responde → A responde`

A resposta antiga não pode substituir:

- slots atuais;
- loading;
- erro;
- seleção correspondente aos parâmetros mais recentes.

A mesma proteção se aplica às mudanças de barbeiro e data.

---

### Histórico protegido

Appointments que a UI já conhece como históricos/protegidos permanecem somente leitura.

A UI não tenta substituir as proteções do backend.

Os casos que dependem de informação não disponível no frontend continuam sendo decididos pelas migrations 027/028.

Nenhuma proteção existente no fluxo de Clients foi enfraquecida.

---

### Local / demo

O fallback local existente foi preservado.

A separação permanece explícita:

**Remote**

`get_owner_availability` é a autoridade de disponibilidade.

**Local/demo**

mantém o comportamento local existente.

Erro remoto não provoca fallback silencioso para cálculo local.

---

### Contratos preservados

Esta PR preserva:

- availability engine da migration 026;
- enforcement transacional da migration 027;
- owner availability RPC da migration 028;
- booking público já aprovado;
- fallback local/demo;
- writers existentes;
- INSERT direto temporário do owner;
- `update_owner_appointment`;
- RLS e grants existentes;
- `financial_timezone`.

Migrations 001–028 permanecem inalteradas.

---

### Validação

Validação final:

- testes focados Vitest: **13 PASS**
- `npm run check`: **467 testes PASS**
- `npm run typecheck`: **PASS**
- `npm run build`: **PASS**
- `npm audit --audit-level=moderate`: **0 vulnerabilidades**
- Playwright owner/barber/public booking: **61 PASS**
- `git diff --check`: **PASS**

A revisão adversarial identificou inicialmente dois achados MEDIUM:

1. barbeiro selecionado na Agenda não era propagado por ID;
2. data inicial remota ainda podia nascer no timezone do navegador.

Ambos foram corrigidos e revisados novamente.

Resultado final da revisão:

**0 BLOCKER**
**0 HIGH**
**0 MEDIUM**

---

### Escopo desta PR

Esta PR integra exclusivamente a UI/repository do owner ao availability engine existente.

Não inclui:

- nova migration;
- alteração das migrations 001–028;
- alteração de RPC;
- alteração de RLS/grants;
- alteração de packages;
- novo writer RPC;
- remoção do INSERT direto do owner;
- alteração de `update_owner_appointment`;
- alteração do `financial_timezone`;
- mudança funcional no booking público;
- deploy ou alteração remota no Supabase.

---

### Riscos residuais

Os E2E utilizam mocks e, portanto, não substituem os testes PostgreSQL/pgTAP do enforcement.

A disponibilidade continua sendo uma fotografia de leitura e não uma reserva.

Entre a leitura e a tentativa de escrita, outro appointment pode ocupar o slot.

Esse comportamento é esperado:

`028 → informa disponibilidade`

`027 → decide atomicamente se a escrita ainda é válida`

O build também mantém o aviso já conhecido de chunk

body:
The Snyk GitHub Actions job was failing because `--all-projects` picked up generated NuGet assets under `obj/`, including a `project.assets.json` path that depends on a missing `PackageOverrides.txt` in the runner’s .NET reference packs. This change narrows the workflow to the actual repository projects and avoids scanning transient build output.

- **Scope the scan to real project manifests**
  - Replace `snyk test --all-projects` / `snyk monitor --all-projects` with explicit scans of:
    - `src/Community.PowerToys.Run.Plugin.Templates.csproj`
    - `tests/Community.PowerToys.Run.Plugin.Templates.Tests.csproj`
  - Store the project list once in workflow env to keep scan targets centralized.

- **Restore the intended solution explicitly**
  - Change restore from repository-wide discovery to `dotnet restore Templates.sln`.
  - Keeps dependency resolution aligned with the template/test solution instead of incidental files in the workspace.

- **Harden failure behavior**
  - Run `test` and `monitor` sequentially per project in PowerShell.
  - Exit immediately on any Snyk command failure rather than continuing through the remaining targets.

```yaml
env:
  SNYK_PROJECTS: |
    src/Community.PowerToys.Run.Plugin.Templates.csproj
    tests/Community.PowerToys.Run.Plugin.Templates.Tests.csproj

- name: Test and monitor
  shell: pwsh
  run: |
    $projects = $env:SNYK_PROJECTS -split "\r?\n" | Where-Object { $_ }

    foreach ($project in $projects) {
      snyk test --file=$project --package-manager=nuget
      if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }

      snyk monitor --file=$project --package-manager=nuget
      if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { exit $LASTEXITCODE }
    }
```

author: adranka
body:
Hello! Thanks for creating this package, it's been very useful for me and recently I've probably been using it daily :smile: 

Firstly, apologies for the large diff in the PR, it was either this or submitting a dozen or so separate PRs. There's a lot of minor implementation detail changes, specifically making things a bit more robust. This PR fixes the following bugs:

1. `cliparray()` crashing on an empty clipboard
2. The output of `mwearray` would give code that chopped off the first row of a matrix. E.g. from the example:
```julia
julia> X = [1 2; 3 4]
2×2 Matrix{Int64}:
 1  2
 3  4

julia> mwearray(X)
X = """
1,2
3,4
""" |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File |> Tables.matrix
julia> X = """
       1,2
       3,4
       """ |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File |> Tables.matrix

1×2 Matrix{Int64}:
 3  4
```
Now `mwearray` outputs `io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)`, which I think is more reasonable:

```julia
julia> mwearray(X)
X = """
1,2
3,4
""" |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)) |> Tables.matrix

julia> X = """
       1,2
       3,4
       """ |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)) |> Tables.matrix
2×2 Matrix{Int64}:
 1  2
 3  4

```

3. Add checks strings to make sure that the payload is properly escaped the MWE functions. Handles backslashes (`\`), interpolation (`$`), quotes (`"`)
```julia
# Current
julia> x = ["C:\\new", "\$CSV", "say \"hi\""]
3-element Vector{String}:
 "C:\\new"
 "\$CSV"
 "say \"hi\""

julia> mwearray(x)
x = """
C:\new
$CSV
"say ""hi"""
""" |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File |> Tables.matrix |> vec
```
```julia
# This PR
julia> mwearray(x)
x = """
C:\\new
\$CSV
\"say \"\"hi\"\"\"
""" |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)) |> Tables.matrix |> vec
julia> 

julia> x = """
       C:\\new
       \$CSV
       \"say \"\"hi\"\"\"
       """ |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)) |> Tables.matrix |> vec
```

4. `mwearray(; name = ...)` would discard the name used
```julia
# Current
julia> mwearray(; name = "some_name")
x = """
1
2
3
""" |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File |> Tables.matrix |> vec

# This PR
julia> mwearray(; name = "some_name")
some_name = """
1
2
3
""" |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; header=false)) |> Tables.matrix |> vec
```

5. If `cliptable(t; newline="\r\n")` was used, it would leave a trailing `\r` at the end of the table.
```julia
julia> t = DataFrame(x = [1, 2, 3])
3×1 DataFrame
 Row │ x     
     │ Int64 
─────┼───────
   1 │     1
   2 │     2
   3 │     3

# Current
julia> cliptable(t; returnstring=true, newline="\r\n")
"x\r\n1\r\n2\r\n3\r"

# This PR
julia> cliptable(t; returnstring=true, newline="\r\n")
"x\r\n1\r\n2\r\n3"
```
6. Apply some macro hygiene and do some more extensive tests on it.
7. Allow forwarding of keyword arguments from `mwearray` and `mwetable` to `cliptable`.
8. Added validating the name when passed into `mwearray` and `mwetable`.
```julia
# Current
julia> mwearray(x; name = "my vector")
my vector = """
1
2
3
""" |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File |> Tables.matrix |> vec

# This PR
julia> mwearray(x; name = "my vector")
ERROR: ArgumentError: `name` must be a valid Julia identifier, got `my vector`.
```

9. Handle tables that have just one column with missing values properly.
```julia
julia> t = (a = [1, missing, 3],)
(a = Union{Missing, Int64}[1, missing, 3],)

# Current
julia> mwetable()
df = """
1
3
""" |> IOBuffer |> CSV.File

# This PR
julia> mwetable(t)
df = """
a
1

3
""" |> IOBuffer |> (io -> CSV.File(io; ignoreemptyrows=false))
```

10. Converted the docstring examples into tests, which are now run in `runtests.jl`.
11. Updated the CI configs. Switched from CompatHelper to Dependabot.
12. Various docstring fixes and clarifications.


These were mostly done by having an AI agent comb through to find issues. Initially I just wanted to see how easy it would be to get CSV.jl 1.0 working and wanted a lot more tests to check against.

Please let me know if you'd prefer seperate PRs over this one mega PR. Thanks!

author: kokhlo
body:
On a cookie-authenticated (OAuth) remote, the Kanban board never received live updates and completion notifications never fired: `pluginSocket` refused to dial when `authMode === 'oauth'` (the "stay on the polling fallback" branch), so the board's only refresh path was the 60 s REST heartbeat — silently, with no UI indication (#117541).

The capability already existed for the app's main gateway socket: main mints a single-use WS ticket per dial (`resolveTestWsUrl` → `mintTicket`), and the server's canonical WS gate (`web_server_chat._ws_auth_ok`, shared by the kanban plugin's `/events` endpoint via `_ws_upgrade_authorized`) accepts `?ticket=` in gated mode. This wires plugin event sockets into that same discipline:

- **`getPluginWsUrl` IPC** (`main.ts` + `preload.ts` + `global.d.ts`): resolves the `(connectionId, profile)` backend, mints when `authMode === 'oauth'` (or uses the static token otherwise), builds the plugin-namespace URL (`connection-config.ts` gains `buildPluginWsUrlWithTicket/WithToken` mirroring `buildGatewayWsUrlWithTicket`), applies the shared-remote profile scope, and remembers the remote's headers for the upgrade — exactly the `freshGatewayWsUrl` recipe. The path is validated plugin-relative (`..` rejected), so the door can't address a core route. Returns `null` when the backend has no usable credential.
- **`pluginSocket` OAuth branch** (`plugins.ts`): dials the minted URL per attempt (tickets are single-use), wiring the same message/backoff handlers as the token path. A rejected mint, a missing bridge (older main process), or a `null` URL keeps the polling fallback — no half-working socket, same behavior as today.
- **Connect-time bail now retries**: `activeConnection()` resolving null previously returned without scheduling anything (the only reconnect path was `socket.onclose`, and there was no socket), so one transient bridge timeout latched the fallback until the next page action. A null connection now goes through the same full-jitter backoff as a closed socket.
- Doc-comment fix in `plugins/kanban/api.ts`: the polls are 60 s board / 30 s drawer, not the stale "8s / 4s" the comment claimed.

Tests (`plugins-oauth.test.ts`): OAuth remote dials the minted URL with `?ticket=`; a rejected mint keeps the polling fallback (no socket opened); the mint request is scoped to the active `(connectionId, profile)`. Existing `plugin-socket-scope.test.ts` and `plugins.test.ts` still pass unchanged (the registry-agent/profile scoping now rides the mint door). RED-verified: the dial and scoping tests fail on unpatched main. `tsc -p .` clean (one pre-existing error on a sparse-checkout fixture, unrelated), eslint clean.

Closes #117541

author: liam-douglas
body:
Two phases of `docs/plan/follow-through.md`. Both are about making fixes stay fixed rather than adding anything new.

## Test what was only ever verified by hand (`8f8ba3c`)

Two behaviours shipped earlier in this run with no automated cover, because the parts that mattered were tangled with code that cannot run in the build environment.

**The feeding editor's date round-trip.** `AnimalDetail`'s inline editor seeded its picker with `log.fed_at.split('T')[0]`, reading a stored ISO string as if it were local: in UTC+10 a 9pm feeding displayed as the next day, and saving anchored it to noon. `isoToDateTimeInput` now lives in `lib/dates.ts` beside its inverse, and the pair is tested as a round-trip — what goes into the picker has to come back out as the same feeding.

The assertions deliberately do not depend on the runner's timezone. CI is in UTC, the keeper is in UTC+10, and a test that only fails in one of those would mislead whoever hits it. The round-trip property catches the original bug in every zone, because slicing discards the time regardless of where you are.

**Sign-out clearing the response cache.** `clearDataCaches` was tested; that sign-out *calls* it was not, because `session.ts` imports the Supabase client and that throws without environment variables. The ordering and failure handling now live in `lib/signOut.ts`, taking their two steps as arguments.

**That extraction found a defect the cache work introduced.** The previous version let a failed sign-out request propagate through its `finally`, so the `navigate` after it never ran — signing out offline stranded the keeper on the settings page with no message and an unhandled rejection. The sequence now returns the failure rather than throwing it, and both callers navigate either way: the point of signing out is to leave, and the local session and caches are cleared whether or not the request reached the server. The failure is said out loud in a toast instead of swallowed.

## Stop the generated types going stale (`a7724cc`)

`docs/schema-types.md` states that the guarantee lapses quietly if a schema change lands without regenerating, and a documented habit is not a guarantee. That lapse would be invisible in exactly the way the drift it guards against was: `schema.ts` would go on checking interfaces against a database that no longer looks like that.

CI cannot reach the database, and does not need to. A pull request touching `supabase/migrations/` without also changing `src/lib/database.types.ts` is either stale or deliberately exempt, and git can tell the difference — no credential to manage, which is worth more here than a check that could read the live schema.

Migrations that genuinely change no columns say so: `0001` (policies and a helper function), `0002` (storage policies) and `0003` (an RPC and a view) carry a `no-schema-change` marker. Forcing a no-op regeneration for those would teach people to regenerate without looking, which is the habit this is meant to build rather than break.

## Verification

Lint, typecheck, build and the suite pass; tests go 113 → 124.

The staleness check was exercised against all four outcomes, and the first against this repository's own history:

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| `0004` added before the types existed (`f3a40f7...e9a5b3f`) | fails, correctly |
| Non-exempt migration touched alone | fails |
| Exempt migration touched alone | passes |
| Non-exempt migration with types regenerated | passes |
| No migration touched | passes |

Note that this PR itself touches three migration files — all three are the exempt ones, so the new job should pass on its own first run, which is a useful thing to watch.

## Not included

Phase 3, extracting `AnimalDetail`'s weight and shedding sections, is deliberately left. It is 1900 lines of JSX that cannot be run here; `tsc` catches a great deal but not a section that renders in the wrong place. The defects it would prevent are hypothetical, unlike the two that slice 1 closed, so the trade did not look worth making blind.

author: matt-evanoff
body:
## What

Adds `requires_llm: ClassVar[bool] = True` to `BaseMetric`. A metric that sets it `False` is constructed without resolving a model from the registry, reports no `model_name` / `llm_provider`, and does not run `LLMHandler._initialize_client`.

## Why

Until now the only way for a metric to say "I don't call a chat model" was to tag itself `heuristic`. That tag takes the right branch in `_set_llm`, but it is also displayed in the registry and read as a claim about *how* the metric decides — so a metric that scores by calling a scoring service with its own non-chat API had to describe itself as a heuristic to get constructed without OpenAI credentials.

The `_initialize_client` skip is the second half. Those two lines write `litellm.api_base` and `litellm.api_key`, which are module globals: a metric that never calls a model was reconfiguring the shared client for every other caller in the process on its way past. This PR stops that for metrics that declare `requires_llm = False`. It does **not** fix it for metrics that do use an LLM — the globals stay global, and that is a separate piece of work.

## Back compatibility

The default is `True`, so every existing metric takes exactly the path it took before. The `heuristic` tag branch is untouched and still works.

## Tests

`tests/metrics/test_requires_llm.py` — 5 tests: the default is `True`; a `requires_llm = False` metric constructs with the registry patched to raise and `OPENAI_API_KEY` unset; it leaves `litellm.api_base` / `api_key` untouched under settings that *would* configure them; a paired control proves an ordinary metric still configures them; and it executes.

- `pytest` → 1363 passed. (`tests/caliber/test_pattern_discovery.py` fails to collect on `master` as well — pre-existing, untouched here.)

The male brain's bytes have been published (#75). This is the line that makes the network serve them.

## On chain already (BSC testnet, from the deployer)

| | |
|---|---|
| `declareLifKind(7209)` | 45,847 gas — **the digest the chain computed is `0x716c4516…3e3e`, which is what this repository's `lifExecKind(7209)` computes** |
| `registerMEP` | 227,925 gas — mepId `0xc17357517fa1…d214`, modelId `0x7a22e8b8…394e`, 166,700 neurons, `weightsDA: gnfd://aigg-brains/malecns-v1.0-min2.bin` |

7209 is 0.40 of FlyWire's 18022: MaleCNS counts the same connections 1.55–1.62× higher, and at 18022 every male stimulus ignites the whole network (`flybnb/male/unit_scan.py`). The relayer asks the chain for a kind's unit, so nothing in `render.yaml` has to repeat it.

## What changes here

- `PORW_MEP_IDS` pins the male base beside the ≥ 5-synapse female export. It belongs to no collection, so the whitelist will never bring it; `PORW_MEP_NAMES` gives it a name.
- `flybnb/male/malecns-v1.0-min2.v3.json` — its profile, the same shape as the gate task's and the genesis base's. `render_blueprint.mjs` checks every pinned id against a profile this repository knows, and now knows where the male one lives.

## Two checks, because a wrong digest is a different brain

**`flybnb_battery.mjs`** ties the profile, the battery and the pinned implementation together: the profile's exec kind is what this `aigg-porw` computes for unit 7209, it is *not* the default kind, and its modelId is the one the male battery's `population` names. Flipping a single hex digit of the recorded `execKind` fails it — checked, not assumed.

**Before pinning anything.** `relayer.mjs` loads pinned MEPs with `await loadMep(id, { pinned: true })` and no `try`/`catch`, so a pinned MEP that cannot be reproduced is not a warning, it is a relayer that does not boot. I ran exactly what `loadMep` does against the live chain for every id this blueprint pins:

ok    0x312dda12d308… unit 18022 reproduces  (gnfd://aigg-brains/flywire-fafb-v783-min5.bin)
ok    0xc17357517fa1… unit 7209  reproduces  (gnfd://aigg-brains/malecns-v1.0-min2.bin)
every pinned MEP loads: the relayer will start

`/meps` gains an entry with `wUnitQ16: 7209` — the first one that is not FlyWire's unit — and the check `post_battery.mjs` does before paying (refuse a brain registered under another unit than the battery's population names) finally has something to be right about. A host that takes the male brain fetches it from the Pages mirror in eight parts; no storage-provider quota is touched.

author: kazu-yamamoto
body:
## What

Twofish put its output together with

```haskell
mapBlocks operation input
    | B.null rest = blockOutput
    | otherwise = blockOutput `B.append` mapBlocks operation rest
  where (block, rest) = B.splitAt blockSize input
```

`B.append` copies everything produced so far, once per block, and `B.splitAt` copies whatever is left of the input — so the message was copied about n/2 times in each direction. On top of that every block went through lists: `load32ls` split the block three times and folded over `B.unpack` to build the four words, `store32ls` built sixteen `Word8`s and packed them.

| message | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 KiB | 1.46 MiB/s | 53 | 36x |
| 1 MiB | 0.30 | 55 | 183x |
| 2 MiB | 0.14 | 56 | **400x** |

Flat in the message length now, where every figure used to get worse the longer the message. Twofish measures above Camellia (39 MiB/s), which is the other Haskell block cipher of its size.

## The change

The block operation is a `Word128 -> Word128` function, as Camellia's already is, and `B.mapAsWord128` walks the input and the output once each. The four little-endian words Twofish works in come out of the two big-endian words `Word128` is read as with `byteSwap32`, which is one instruction.

`mapBlocks`, `load32ls` and `store32ls` are internal to `Crypto.Cipher.Twofish.Primitive`, which is not an exposed module.

## Tests

Every vector in the suite is one block long, and the loop that walks the blocks is what this changes. The first commit says what ECB is: a message of five blocks is its blocks encrypted one at a time and put back together, the same going back, and 64 KiB still decrypts to itself. Those pass before the rewrite as well as after.

`cabal test`: 2505 examples, 0 failures.

## One behaviour change

Input that is not a whole number of blocks now raises, as it does for AES and DES. It used to come back **longer than it went in**: the short block was read as though the bytes it does not have were zero, and a whole block was written out. A test in the second commit pins the refusal.

author: pofallon
body:
Sibling to **try-hola/hola#491** (spec 007, restore-on-install). That PR builds the install-side machinery; this one tells it what a restore *means* for each app.

The platform half works without this — 12 of the 17 apps here restore by plain file copy today — so the two can land independently. The five Postgres-backed apps need both.

## What an app declares

`accepts: ["restore@1"]` marks an app restorable. A `restore` block adds per-participation detail. **The two states are meaningfully different:**

| Declaration | Meaning |
|---|---|
| no `restore@1` | nobody has considered restoring this app — not offered as a source |
| `restore@1`, no block | **plain file copy is all it needs** — true for every SQLite/flat-file app here |
| `restore@1` + block | discards and/or a hook apply |

The middle state already exists in this catalog: twelve apps declare `accepts: ["backup@1"]` with no hooks. This change gives that shape a meaning rather than asking anyone to adopt a new one.

## Why `discard` exists

It's the non-obvious field, and the reason these five need more than a copy.

A file-level tar of a **live** Postgres data directory is read over minutes while the database writes throughout — page 1 at T+0s, page 100000 at T+180s. That's a smear across time, not a snapshot, and for Postgres a smear is corruption. Hola's own capture helper concedes as much: it suppresses tar's *"file changed as we read it"* warning because crash-consistency is all it promises.

The `.sql` dump is the real payload, and it's already captured — all five apps dump into `${HOLA_APP_DATA}/backups`, inside the data root. So: discard the smeared data directory, let the container `initdb` a clean cluster, load the dump into it.

## Per-app

| App | hook service | `discard` | healthcheck already declared |
|---|---|---|---|
| guacamole | `postgres` | `postgres` | ✅ |
| immich | `immich-postgres` | `postgres` | ✅ |
| mealie | `mealie-postgres` | `postgres` | ✅ |
| paperless-ngx | `db` | **`pgdata`** | ✅ |
| postiz | `postiz-postgres` | `postgres` | ✅ |

**Every `discard` path was read from that app's own `compose.yaml`, not copied between apps.** paperless-ngx mounts `pgdata` where the other four mount `postgres` — and a wrong path here fails *silently*, discarding nothing and restoring the smear.

Every hook carries **`-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`**. Without it `psql` exits 0 after a failed statement, which would hand a partially loaded database to an app that then migrates it — exactly the corruption the server's fail-closed hook policy exists to prevent.

Hola waits on each hook service's **own declared healthcheck** (`docker compose up -d --wait <svc>`) rather than a bespoke readiness poll, since per-app readiness knowledge in the server is what its generic-primitive rule forbids. All five already declare one, so no compose change was needed.

## Schema

Additive. `restore` is a new optional array; `hook` reuses the existing `$defs/backupHook` rather than introducing a second hook format.

`restore@1` joins the `contractRef` enum, and that enum's description is extended to record **the one thing that makes it different from its neighbours**: it is *not* a brokered capability contract. Hola's `CONTRACTS` registry gains no entry for it, and the server never brokers it between two parties — it only says "this app has considered being restored." The enum stays closed for the reason it always was: the server drops an unrecognised ref with a warning, so an open enum would turn a typo into a silent no-op instead of a CI failure.

## Verification

All 17 manifests in this catalog validate against the updated schema (`ajv`), unchanged ones included.

**Not yet exercised against real containers.** The end-to-end pass — a real restore of one of these five, with the captured data directory discarded and the dump loaded — needs a published bundle carrying these declarations, so it runs after this merges. That gap is called out on try-hola/hola#491 too.

Windows network-path classification replaced every forward slash in an input before inspecting its prefix. Path admission and filename sanitization separately implemented the same ASCII drive-prefix grammar. Share those small syntax primitives and inspect the network prefix directly, removing the full-input allocation and 29 production code lines.

Caller policies remain distinct: question-mark rooted drives are local, dot namespaces remain network paths, and relative alias admission rejects every colon. Raw path suffixes and the existing public drive-letter predicate's coercion remain unchanged.

Build, package/API checks, both lints, 268 focused tests, and 296,504 independent prefix/generated/long-input comparisons passed. Final managed review is clean through P2. The complete CI, coverage, benchmarks and CodeQL runs passed at rebased head 19b8a6a9ee42f5c190b57e47484d69a0931bf814, including real Windows native and fallback execution: 25 passed checks, 5 conditional skips, no reruns.

An isolated Node 24 comparison on AWS Crabbox cbx_420265048ad6 (c7a.4xlarge, 16 vCPU) independently built da457e0 against d7c79ee and ran balanced ABBA/BAAB blocks with varying inputs and correctness assertions. The four changed production files and regression test are byte-identical after rebasing onto the landed deny-policy cleanup; only a changelog conflict needed resolution. This measures JavaScript predicates on Linux with the explicit Windows-platform argument; it does not measure end-to-end Windows filesystem performance.

| Predicate and input | Base | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Network classification, short local backslash path | 39.25 ns | 3.31 ns |
| Network classification, short UNC backslash path | 42.59 ns | 10.83 ns |
| Internal alias check, rooted local path | 19.81 ns | 22.87 ns |
| Unchanged public drive predicate control | 17.42 ns | 17.38 ns |

The timing harness imported freshly built `dist/advanced.js` directly; package installation was validated separately in CI. The squash message's phrase "installed-artifact predicate timings" is inaccurate and should read "compiled-artifact predicate timings".

Normal network-path inputs improved in the complete mixed-input run as well, by 2.4–48.7× depending on prefix/slashes. The internal rooted-local alias predicate has a small measured cost of about 3 ns; extended alias checks were faster. The original mixed run showed an unchanged drive control +3.14 ns; one bounded fresh-process follow-up made that control neutral while retaining the rooted-alias cost. Both datasets are retained. The lease is verified released.

author: comradezephyr
body:
## Summary

Adds an active scan script that detects CVE-2025-29927, a critical (CVSS 9.1)
authorization bypass in Next.js. Next.js uses the `x-middleware-subrequest`
request header to identify its own internal subrequests and, in vulnerable
versions, trusts it without verifying that the request originated internally.
Supplying the header causes the application's middleware to be skipped
entirely, bypassing any authentication, authorization or redirect logic
implemented there.

Fixed in Next.js 12.3.5, 13.5.9, 14.2.25 and 15.2.3.

## What the script does

- Only tests `GET` nodes, and only continues when the baseline response looks
  gated by middleware (301/302/303/307/308, 401 or 403). Resources returning
  200 are skipped, since public and protected responses cannot be
  distinguished.
- Repeats the request with each known `x-middleware-subrequest` value
  (`middleware` x5, `src/middleware` x5, `middleware`, `src/middleware`,
  `pages/_middleware`). The x5 values are needed for Next.js 13.2 and later,
  where the middleware module name must appear five times
  (MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH).
- Confirms a bypass only when the gate is gone: a 200 response that differs
  from the baseline and does not look like a login page. 5xx responses are
  ignored.
- Raises High risk / Medium confidence when Next.js response headers are
  present, downgrading to Low confidence when they are not (they are trivial
  to hide), so weaker findings do not pollute high-confidence reports.
- Follows the `getMetadata()` / `ScanRuleMetadata.fromYaml` pattern already
  used by `active/SSTI.js` and `active/OpenModelContextProtocolServer.js`.

Metadata: `id: 100046`, CWE-287 (Improper Authentication), WASC-1,
OWASP Top 10 2021 A01 / 2017 A02 alert tags, `status: alpha`.

## How it was tested

- `node --check` on the script: pass
- `./gradlew spotlessCheck` (same check CI runs): pass
- Repo test suite `VerifyScripts` (parses every script with GraalJS):
  182 tests, 182 successful, 0 failed, including
  `TEST-DONE active\CVE202529927.js -> SUCCESSFUL`
- Behavioural harness against scripted mock servers covering 13 scenarios
  (vulnerable, patched, SPA shell, SSO gateway, public page, 401 gate,
  same-size response, 5xx, hidden Next.js headers, POST skip, de-duplication,
  `scan()` no-op, metadata): 43 checks, 0 failed
- `getMetadata()` YAML validated with SnakeYAML (the parser ZAP uses):
  all 14 keys and references parsed correctly

I have not yet run a live end-to-end scan inside ZAP against a real Next.js
deployment; the verification above is at the script level. Happy to run it
against a lab target and report results if that would help.

## References

- https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-29927
- https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-f82v-jwr5-mffw
- https://zhero-web-sec.github.io/research-and-things/nextjs-and-cve-2025-29927-a-new-vulnerability

## Notes

This is my first contribution to ZAP. Feedback on style and conventions is
welcome. I chose `100046` as the scan rule ID after checking the IDs already
used by the community scripts (highest existing is `100045`); happy to change
it if another is preferred.

While preparing this I noticed that `./gradlew check` fails on Windows
because `VerifyScripts.readFiles()` filters the classpath with
`endsWith("/scripts")` while Gradle passes a path with backslashes on
Windows. It fails before reading any script file. CI runs on Linux so it is
unaffected. I did not touch that file; mentioning it in case it is worth a
separate issue.

author: juanlentino
body:
Closes #1606

## What

Three seams in the SN command palette move onto the station's own mechanisms; the classic wp-admin behaviour outside the station is unchanged.

- `toast()` in `assets/desktop-mode.js` calls `wp.os.showToast( { message } )` (Stable) and returns the message. Every `run()` returns its promise chain, so the palette paints the verdict as the command's answer. The wp.data and console fallbacks stay for a shell without `showToast`.
- `navigate( url, ctx, title )` keeps the same-origin check, then tries `window.sntOpenStationPreferences.tryNativeRemap( url )` (the plugin's own `wp.os.openWindow` opener, preference-gated) and closes the palette when it takes the URL; otherwise `ctx.openInWindow( url, title )` (CommandContext, Stable). `location.href` is gone. The nine open commands pass `ctx` through.
- Full reset asks `wp.os.confirm( { title, message, confirmLabel, danger: true } )` (Stable), with `sntConfirm` as the fallback for a shell without `confirm` and no `window.confirm` anywhere.
- One guard at the top of `sntConfirm()` in `assets/snt-confirm.js` returns `wp.os.confirm()` when the shell has it, so every caller, imperative (the Cron leaf's Run now and Unschedule) and declarative (`[data-snt-confirm]`), gets the station's dialog. An iframe window's `wp.os` carries no `confirm`, so classic pages and chromeless windows keep the modal.

## Why

Read against OpenStation v1.1.10 source and docs. `wp.os.notify` is the PWA browser-notification entry; its first guard drops any intent without a `title` (`src/pwa/notify.ts:95`), so all 30 toasts were silent and 15 of the 22 commands showed nothing since upstream #705 made them run. `run()` returned nothing, so the palette's answer surface stayed empty. `location.href` on the shell document is a top-frame load that `admin_init` redirects back into the shell, rebooting the desktop and restoring the session. `snt-confirm` is never enqueued on the shell, so Full reset landed on `window.confirm`, the call the shell's lint forbids; inside the S&N Home window two different confirm dialogs sat in one window.

Seam status (OpenStation `docs/javascript-reference.md`): `showToast` Stable (:2741), `ctx.openInWindow` Stable on the CommandContext (:2928), `wp.os.confirm` Stable (:21). `ctx.confirm( message, details )` was not used because the default `_confirm` drops `confirmLabel` and `danger` (`src/ai-assistant/impl.ts:967-972`).

Skipped: the optional hygiene of dropping `snt-confirm` from the analytics window's script list (a separate pin moves with it; not in the three cuts).

## Verified

- `tests/js/desktop-mode-boot.mjs` executes the real file against a recording shell: one `showToast` call with `message` and zero `notify`; `run()` returns the message; the remap takes the URL and closes the palette with no `openInWindow` and `location.href` untouched; when the remap declines, `openInWindow` opens the page; Full reset asks `wp.os.confirm` with `danger: true` and `confirmLabel: 'Full Reset'`, never `window.confirm`, and answers "Full reset cancelled." on No. Mirrored in `tests/desktop-mode-boot-order.php`.
- `tests/desktop-mode-integration.php` reads the comment-stripped sources: no `location.href`, no `window.confirm(`, `showToast` and no `.notify(`, remap before `openInWindow`; `snt-confirm.js` reads `wp.os.confirm` before it builds the backdrop and forwards `danger`.
- **Red count: 11** against the unfixed files (`git show origin/main:` swapped in, run, restored): 5 executed scenarios in `desktop-mode-boot-order.php` (plus its exit-code mirror, 6 lines) and 6 source pins in `desktop-mode-integration.php`. Green after the fix.
- `bash tests/run.sh` for `desktop-mode-integration.php` (587), `desktop-mode-boot-order.php` (17), `ability-run-client.php` (39), `desktop-mode-attention.php` (43), `openstation-host-assets.php` (171), `openstation-host.php` (127), `openstation-app.php` (123): all green. Full sweep green.
- phpcs (`phpcs.xml.dist`) clean on both touched PHP suites. `node --check` on both JS files.

body:
## Item 6 do backlog de segurança

O rate-limit dos agentes de IA públicos (`concierge`, `orcamento`, `upsell`) era só em memória — resetava a cada cold start e era por instância.

### O que mudou
- **`ai.js`**: além do rate-limit em memória, agora faz um rate-limit **persistente e compartilhado** entre instâncias — contador **por hora e por IP** no Realtime Database via **incremento atômico** (`{".sv":{"increment":1}}`), escrito com o Database Secret (ignora as regras). Qualquer um dos dois que estoure → 429. **Fail-open** se o DB não responder (os tetos de orçamento por agente e o rate-limit em memória seguem valendo).
- **`ai-dispatcher.js`**: limpa diariamente os buckets `aiRateLimit` de dias anteriores (usa `shallow=true` para baixar só as chaves).
- **`database.rules.json` / README**: regra `aiRateLimit` (admin) para least-privilege/observabilidade.

### Testes
21 chamadas do mesmo IP ao `concierge` → a 21ª retorna **429**; IP diferente não é bloqueado.

author: ftounga
body:
## Ce que ça corrige

Trois défauts relevés par le PO sur les budgets de F-133, sur le même écran — donc une seule PR.

### SF-133-12 — L'alerte là où l'on travaille

SF-133-06 avait placé les alertes dans la console d'administration, et le cadrage l'assumait :
*« un bandeau dans la console d'admin, et rien ailleurs »*. **C'était le mauvais choix** : une alerte
qu'il faut aller chercher n'alerte personne.

Un bandeau apparaît désormais en tête de `/forge`, l'écran de travail. « Masquer » le retire **pour
la session** ; il revient à la connexion suivante — et plus tôt si la situation s'aggrave (on
approchait, on a dépassé). Une erreur d'API n'affiche **rien** : une alerte est un confort, elle ne
doit jamais abîmer l'écran.

**Ouvert à tous, chiffré pour l'administrateur seul.** `GET /api/cost/alerts/mine` n'exige pas le
rôle admin — l'isolation passe par `user_id` — mais `spentEur` et `budgetEur` sont **retirés du
JSON** pour qui ne l'est pas. Absents, pas masqués : masqués, ils resteraient lisibles dans le flux
réseau. Le pourcentage reste visible pour tous : il dit l'ampleur sans dire l'argent.

### SF-133-13 — Tous les clients budgétables

> *« Pourquoi le seul client sur qui je peux mettre le budget de la semaine c'est CAGIP ? »*

La liste venait de `usage_turns` **sur la fenêtre** : un client qui n'avait pas travaillé cette
semaine n'apparaissait pas, donc n'avait pas de champ « Budget ». Or c'est précisément **avant**
qu'un client dépense qu'on veut lui poser un plafond. Le résumé liste maintenant tous les postes non
clôturés, à zéro, avec leur nom.

### SF-133-14 — Le budget par défaut expliqué

> *« On est d'accord, c'est celui pour tous les clients, mélangé sur toute la semaine ? »*

**Non** — et c'était le problème. Le montant s'applique **à chaque client** sans budget propre : deux
clients à 50 € plafonnent la semaine à 100 €. Le libellé dit désormais « par client », une note écrit
la règle, et le plafond résultant est affiché — **lu du résumé**, jamais recalculé côté navigateur.

## Tests

| | |
|---|---|
| Backend | **4213**, 0 échec (dont 4 d'intégration sur la nouvelle route, 5 sur le résumé) |
| Frontend | **2335**, 0 échec (dont 9 sur le bandeau, 4 sur l'écran admin) |
| Build | `npm run build` vert |
| Migration | **aucune** — pas de schéma touché |

## Checklists

- Readiness : **PASS** (affichée dans la conversation)
- Review : **PASS** — une dérive assumée, le bandeau va dans `PostesComponent` (`/forge`) et non
  `MesClientsComponent` (`/forge/clients`) comme la mini-spec le prévoyait : c'est l'écran de travail.
  Mini-spec corrigée.
- Release : **PASS**

## Summary

Fixes a pre-existing, order-dependent test pair in `tests/test_key_durability.py`, found while comparing #376's full-suite results against `main` and traced in `_internal/work-docs/mlv16-orchestration/SIGNING_KEY_CACHE_TEST_ISOLATION.md`.

`nce/signing.py`'s module-level `_key_cache` (a `TTLCache`, documented as unlocked and never reset between tests) is process-wide. An autouse `conftest.py` fixture already existed to clear it after each test, but only did so for tests carrying an opt-in `signing_isolation` marker — about 24 tests used it. Measured before choosing a fix: at least 6 more files call the real, unmocked `get_active_key` without that marker, including `test_key_durability.py`, any of which could leave stale cache state behind for whatever test runs next in a full-suite run.

## What changed

- `tests/conftest.py`: `_reset_signing_key_cache_after_test` now clears the cache unconditionally after every test, instead of only when the `signing_isolation` marker is present.
- Removed the now-dead marker: `pytest.ini`'s registration, the module-level `pytestmark` in `tests/test_signing_cache.py`, and the three `@pytest.mark.signing_isolation` decorators in `tests/test_health_probes.py`.

No test needed the marker's absence — checked directly: every real cache-populating test populates and asserts within its own body, and `test_master_key_buffer.py`'s direct cache-object substitution restores the original in a `finally` block before finishing.

## Test plan

- [x] Reproduced the order-dependent pair, then confirmed the fix closes it: full `tests/` suite run before the fix (9 failed, including exactly one of the two `test_key_durability.py` tests) vs. after (7 failed, neither `test_key_durability.py` test present — the remaining 7 are pre-existing and unrelated, confirmed identical to a fresh `origin/main` run)

author: scholtz
body:
## Summary
- go-algorand `v5.0.2-stable` added a stateless `wellFormed()` bound check on `unauthenticatedVote`/`unauthenticatedBundle` rejecting any step greater than `down` (the largest step the protocol defines). Before this, algod-rust would decode and forward a vote/bundle/proposal with an absurdly large step value (e.g. `u64::MAX`), only rejecting it later in the pipeline if at all.
- Adds `UnauthenticatedVote::well_formed()` / `UnauthenticatedBundle::well_formed()`, called both at decode time (`Demux::handle_raw_vote`/`handle_raw_bundle`/`handle_raw_proposal` — the equivalent of Go's `decodeVote`/`decodeBundle`/`decodeProposal`, disconnecting the peer like any other malformed decode) and again inside `verify()`, as defense in depth, matching Go's structure exactly.
- Updates `docs/phase17/parity_agreement.md`: `TestBundleVerifyRejectsStepAboveDown`, `TestVoteVerifyRejectsStepAboveDown`, and `TestDecodeRejectsStepAboveDown` all moved from `unclassified` placeholders to `matched-*` rows linking the new tests. `python3 scripts/update_phase17_summary.py` is deferred to whichever PR in this epic (#1547) closes the last remaining `unclassified` row — the script refuses to run while any row anywhere is still `unclassified`, and 6 rows remain, owned by sibling issues #1544/#1545/#1546.

Fixes #1543. Part of epic #1547.

## Test plan
- New unit tests: `bundle_verify_rejects_step_above_down`, `bundle_well_formed_step_bound`, `vote_verify_rejects_step_above_down`, `vote_well_formed_step_bound`, `demux_raw_vote_with_step_above_down_is_dropped_and_disconnects`, `demux_raw_bundle_with_step_above_down_is_dropped_and_disconnects`, `demux_raw_proposal_with_prior_vote_step_above_down_is_dropped_and_disconnects` — all pass, and fail against the pre-fix code (verified by temporarily reverting `well_formed()`'s call sites).
- `cargo fmt --all`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo test --workspace` — clean except one confirmed-flaky multi-node timing test (`certificate_does_not_stall_single_relay_five_node`, fails only under full-suite parallel load, passes in isolation, untouched by this diff) and the pre-existing `pq_falcon_e2e_test` failures (confirmed pre-existing on `main` before this branch, unrelated Falcon PQ e2e code).
- Live mixed-cluster verification: not run for this PR — the change is a pure input-validation tightening on a step value that no real go-algorand or algod-rust node ever produces out-of-range in practice; the new unit/decode-path tests are the practical way to exercise it (constructing a genuinely out-of-bound step requires hand-crafting the wire message, exactly what the new tests do).

author: octobercomms
body:
Second Phase-1 item from `docs/omi/recorder-polish-roadmap.md`. The recorder captures **WebM only**, which is a compatibility footgun the moment a video is downloaded or handed to another tool. Staff can now render a shareable **H.264 MP4** (or a short **GIF**) from any recording, server-side.

### How it works
- **migration 173** — adds `recordings.mp4_key` / `gif_key` / `export_status`.
- **`services/recordingExport.js`** — fire-and-forget ffmpeg render (like the transcription worker). MP4 = standard `libx264` / `aac` / `+faststart`; GIF = two-pass `palettegen` → `paletteuse` at 12fps/720px. Output goes back into the same media store; ffmpeg resolved from `FFMPEG_PATH` (same as `editProcessor.js`).
- **`routes/recordings.js`** — `POST /:id/export {format}` (owner-scoped) kicks the render; `GET /:id/download?format=` streams the asset (disk pipe, or R2 signed-URL redirect); `present()` exposes `has_mp4` / `has_gif` / `export_status`; delete + bulk-delete now also remove the rendered assets.
- **`RecordingsPage.jsx`** — per-recording **MP4 / GIF** buttons: render → shows `…` while processing (library polls every 4s) → becomes a **⬇ download**.

Fully **additive and opt-in** — existing recordings render byte-identically until someone clicks Export; no existing flow changes.

### Verification
- `node -c` on both backend files; `vite build` passes.
- ffmpeg commands are the standard, widely-used forms. **Note:** I could not run ffmpeg in this environment, so the render output itself is unverified at runtime — but it's contained (a failed render sets `export_status='failed'` and can't affect the source recording or any other flow). Worth a quick real-world export check.
